title: Weighing alternatives: cost in real decisions

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Analyse how opportunity cost influences the decisions of consumers, workers, producers and governments: what is weighed against what, and when a choice is worthwhile.

blocks.heading: The weighing that decides
blocks.text: A decision maker does not ask what a choice costs in money alone; the question is what the same effort would have earned elsewhere. The method: list the realistic alternatives, rank them by expected benefit, choose the best - and the opportunity cost is the expected benefit of the runner-up. A choice tends to be worthwhile when the benefit of what is chosen exceeds the benefit of that runner-up. Note what this is not: the decision to choose is the act of picking; the opportunity cost is the measured sacrifice that act creates. The two work together - the cost is what the decision is weighed against.

blocks.heading: The chain from cost to behaviour
blocks.text: Because the runner-up benefit is the benchmark, a change in it changes the choice. Starting point: a worker at Oshakati Textiles is offered a Saturday shift paying N$420, and her next best use of the Saturday is mending stock for her market stall, worth N$300 to her. Mechanism: the shift pays more than the forgone alternative, so she takes it, because the N$300 is what the Saturday really costs her. If stall trade improves and the Saturday of mending rises to N$500 in value, the same shift now costs more than it pays, and the scales tip the other way. Consequence: she declines the shift, the factory loses a willing worker, and her stall keeps the sales. The cost did not change the pay; it changed the comparison, and the comparison decides.

blocks.heading: Four decision makers, one logic
blocks.text: A consumer in Windhoek with N$120 spends it on data and gives up the taxi rides the same N$120 would have bought. Kaoko Juice runs its one bottling line on mango nectar and gives up the marula batch worth N$18 000 the line would have filled. The government of a town near Gobabis spends its N$1.5 million road fund on the tarred link to the main road and gives up the clinic upgrade the same money would have funded. In Germany, a city council weighing a new tram line against extra school places runs the identical comparison. Each decision maker weighs benefit against forgone benefit - that is the influence of opportunity cost on decision making.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Workers weighing pay against other uses of their time reappear in topic 3.3, and governments weighing one spending use against another are the budget choices of topic 4.1.
